difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: EASY because it needs one concept (the product rule $\det(AB) = \det A \det B$ after factoring $M^2 + 12M = M(M + 12I)$) plus a single $3 \times 3$ determinant that is visibly zero (row 3 = row 1 + row 2), so a prepared student finishes in about a minute.
stem:
Consider the $3 \times 3$ matrix $\boldsymbol{M} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 3 \\ 4 & 3 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$.

The determinant of $(\boldsymbol{M}^2 + 12\boldsymbol{M})$ is ______.

solution.quick: Factor $\boldsymbol{M}^2 + 12\boldsymbol{M} = \boldsymbol{M}(\boldsymbol{M} + 12\boldsymbol{I})$, so $\det(\boldsymbol{M}^2 + 12\boldsymbol{M}) = \det(\boldsymbol{M})\,\det(\boldsymbol{M} + 12\boldsymbol{I})$. Row 3 of $\boldsymbol{M}$ is row 1 + row 2 ($[4, 3, 6] = [1, 2, 3] + [3, 1, 3]$), so $\det \boldsymbol{M} = 0$ and the whole product is $0$. Answer: **0**.

steps.title: Formula: factor the matrix polynomial
steps.body:
Matrix multiplication distributes over addition, and $\boldsymbol{M}$ commutes with $\boldsymbol{I}$, so

$$\boldsymbol{M}^2 + 12\boldsymbol{M} = \boldsymbol{M}\boldsymbol{M} + \boldsymbol{M}(12\boldsymbol{I}) = \boldsymbol{M}(\boldsymbol{M} + 12\boldsymbol{I}).$$

By the product rule for determinants, $\det(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B}) = \det(\boldsymbol{A})\det(\boldsymbol{B})$:

$$\det(\boldsymbol{M}^2 + 12\boldsymbol{M}) = \det(\boldsymbol{M})\cdot\det(\boldsymbol{M} + 12\boldsymbol{I}).$$

steps.title: Calculate $\det(\boldsymbol{M})$ by cofactor expansion
steps.body:
Expanding along the first row of $\boldsymbol{M} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 3 \\ 4 & 3 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$:

$$\det \boldsymbol{M} = 1\,(1\cdot 6 - 3\cdot 3) - 2\,(3\cdot 6 - 3\cdot 4) + 3\,(3\cdot 3 - 1\cdot 4)$$

$$= 1(6 - 9) - 2(18 - 12) + 3(9 - 4) = -3 - 12 + 15 = 0.$$

The reason is visible in the rows: $R_3 = [4, 3, 6] = [1, 2, 3] + [3, 1, 3] = R_1 + R_2$. The rows are linearly dependent, so $\operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol{M}) = 2 < 3$ and $\boldsymbol{M}$ is singular.

steps.title: Combine: the product is zero
steps.body:
Since $\det \boldsymbol{M} = 0$,

$$\det(\boldsymbol{M}^2 + 12\boldsymbol{M}) = 0 \cdot \det(\boldsymbol{M} + 12\boldsymbol{I}) = 0,$$

whatever the value of the second factor. (For completeness, $\boldsymbol{M} + 12\boldsymbol{I} = \begin{bmatrix} 13 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 13 & 3 \\ 4 & 3 & 18 \end{bmatrix}$ has determinant $13(234 - 9) - 2(54 - 12) + 3(9 - 52) = 2925 - 84 - 129 = 2712 \ne 0$, but multiplying by $0$ still gives $0$.)

steps.title: Cross-check by direct computation
steps.body:
$$\boldsymbol{M}^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 19 & 13 & 27 \\ 18 & 16 & 30 \\ 37 & 29 & 57 \end{bmatrix}, \quad 12\boldsymbol{M} = \begin{bmatrix} 12 & 24 & 36 \\ 36 & 12 & 36 \\ 48 & 36 & 72 \end{bmatrix},$$

$$\boldsymbol{M}^2 + 12\boldsymbol{M} = \begin{bmatrix} 31 & 37 & 63 \\ 54 & 28 & 66 \\ 85 & 65 & 129 \end{bmatrix}.$$

Its third row is again the sum of the first two ($31 + 54 = 85$, $37 + 28 = 65$, $63 + 66 = 129$), so its determinant is $0$. The Python check confirms $\det(\boldsymbol{M}^2 + 12\boldsymbol{M}) = 0$.

**Final answer: 0**

solution.teaching:
**What a determinant measures.** For a square matrix $\boldsymbol{A}$, $\det \boldsymbol{A}$ is the factor by which the linear map $\boldsymbol{x} \mapsto \boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}$ scales volume. If the columns (equivalently, the rows) are linearly dependent, the map squashes space onto a lower-dimensional subspace, the volume becomes zero and $\det \boldsymbol{A} = 0$. So a quick test is: *can one row (or column) be written as a combination of the others?* If yes, the determinant is $0$ and the rank is less than $n$.

**The product rule.** Applying $\boldsymbol{B}$ and then $\boldsymbol{A}$ scales volume by $\det \boldsymbol{B}$ and then by $\det \boldsymbol{A}$, which is why $\det(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B}) = \det(\boldsymbol{A})\det(\boldsymbol{B})$. There is **no** such rule for sums: in general $\det(\boldsymbol{A} + \boldsymbol{B}) \ne \det \boldsymbol{A} + \det \boldsymbol{B}$. So when you see a polynomial in one matrix, such as $\boldsymbol{M}^2 + 12\boldsymbol{M}$, the move is to **factor** it into a product first. Polynomials in the same matrix commute with each other, so $\boldsymbol{M}^2 + 12\boldsymbol{M} = \boldsymbol{M}(\boldsymbol{M} + 12\boldsymbol{I})$, just like $x^2 + 12x = x(x + 12)$.

**The eigenvalue view.** If $\boldsymbol{M}$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3$, then $p(\boldsymbol{M})$ has eigenvalues $p(\lambda_i)$ and $\det p(\boldsymbol{M}) = \prod_i p(\lambda_i)$. Here $p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 + 12\lambda = \lambda(\lambda + 12)$. A singular $\boldsymbol{M}$ has an eigenvalue $0$, and $p(0) = 0$, so the product is $0$. (The characteristic polynomial of this $\boldsymbol{M}$ is $\lambda^3 - 8\lambda^2 - 14\lambda$, with eigenvalues $0$ and $4 \pm \sqrt{30}$.)

**Back to this question.** Row 3 of $\boldsymbol{M}$ equals row 1 + row 2, so $\det \boldsymbol{M} = 0$. Because $\det(\boldsymbol{M}^2 + 12\boldsymbol{M}) = \det(\boldsymbol{M})\det(\boldsymbol{M} + 12\boldsymbol{I})$, the answer is $0$ without computing any product of matrices.
solution.shortcut: Before multiplying anything, check whether $\boldsymbol{M}$ is singular. Here $[4, 3, 6] = [1, 2, 3] + [3, 1, 3]$, so $\det \boldsymbol{M} = 0$, and any matrix of the form $\boldsymbol{M}\cdot(\text{something})$, including $\boldsymbol{M}^2 + 12\boldsymbol{M} = \boldsymbol{M}(\boldsymbol{M} + 12\boldsymbol{I})$, also has determinant $0$.
solution.commonTrap: Treating the determinant as additive, i.e. writing $\det(\boldsymbol{M}^2 + 12\boldsymbol{M}) = (\det \boldsymbol{M})^2 + 12\det \boldsymbol{M}$ or $(\det \boldsymbol{M})^2 + 12^3\det \boldsymbol{M}$. That rule does not exist; it happens to give 0 here only because $\det \boldsymbol{M} = 0$, and it fails in general. A second trap is grinding out $\boldsymbol{M}^2 + 12\boldsymbol{M}$ entry by entry and then making an arithmetic slip in the $3 \times 3$ determinant of large numbers; spotting that $\boldsymbol{M}$ is singular avoids all of that work.

answerVerification.method: Author solve (not blind) compared with official key
answerVerification.checkCode:
import sympy as sp
M = sp.Matrix([[1,2,3],[3,1,3],[4,3,6]])
print(M.det())                       # 0  (row3 = row1 + row2)
assert M.row(2) == M.row(0) + M.row(1)
N = M**2 + 12*M
print(N)                             # [[31,37,63],[54,28,66],[85,65,129]]
print(N.det())                       # 0
A = M + 12*sp.eye(3)
print(A.det())                       # 2712 (non-zero, irrelevant: 0*2712 = 0)
assert N == M*A and N.det() == M.det()*A.det() == 0
print(M.charpoly().as_expr(), M.eigenvals())   # l^3-8l^2-14l ; {0, 4+-sqrt(30)}
print([sp.simplify(l**2 + 12*l) for l in M.eigenvals()])  # eigenvalues of N; one is 0
answerVerification.notes: M^2 + 12M = M(M + 12I), so det(M^2 + 12M) = det(M) det(M + 12I). Row 3 of M equals row 1 + row 2, so det(M) = 0 (cofactor expansion: -3 - 12 + 15 = 0) and the product is 0, although det(M + 12I) = 2712. Direct computation in sympy gives M^2 + 12M = [[31,37,63],[54,28,66],[85,65,129]] with determinant 0. This agrees with the official key 0 to 0.
